justification: No factual error found. run-code passed 3/3 with identical output (blocks=20, executed=10), matching the writer's claim exactly. I hand-traced all five algorithms against the actual code and the printed output, recomputing every Gantt slice and every turnaround/wait/response number from scratch rather than trusting the article's arithmetic: FCFS (avg 12.2/7.8/7.8), SJF (9.6/5.2/5.2, correctly picking P5 then P2 then P4 then P3 once arrived), RR q=4 (13.8/9.4/5.4, verified slice-by-slice including the arrivals-before-returning-process admission order), priority (11.4/7.0/7.0), and MLFQ (13.6/9.2/4.0) all reproduce exactly by hand — the simulator is correct, not just plausible. The RR quantum-sweep exercise is genuinely correct: I traced q=2 by hand tick-by-tick and got 14.2/9.8/2.8, matching the article precisely, and confirmed q=8 (>= the longest burst, so no job is ever preempted) produces exactly the FCFS numbers because dispatch order becomes arrival order — real degeneration to FCFS, not an assertion. The aging exercise is genuinely correct: static priority strands P1 at turnaround 10; under aging (effective = Priority - waited), P1's effective priority falls to 1 at clock=4, ties P4 (also effective 1) on the arrival tie-break, and wins because P1 arrived earlier — a real flipped decision, turnaround 10 to 6, exactly as claimed. The MLFQ implementation was checked tick-by-tick against the real OSTEP rules: I pulled the actual chapter-8 PDF text with pdftotext (WebFetch cannot parse the PDF binary) and confirmed the book's final five-rule summary reads, verbatim, 'Rule 1: If Priority(A) > Priority(B), A runs... Rule 4: Once a job uses up its time allotment at a given level (regardless of how many times it has given up the CPU), its priority is reduced... Rule 5: After some time period S, move all the jobs in the system to the topmost queue' — the article's paraphrase matches this exactly, and the simulator's demotion (P1 drops to level 1 at t=3 after its level-0 quantum of 3) and boost (every waiting/running job jumps back to level 0 at t=14, which visibly erases P1's and P3's demotions in the trace) are both present and correctly gated on 'used its whole allotment' rather than on voluntary yields, matching Rule 4's anti-gaming intent. I also confirmed from the same PDF that OSTEP's own definitions (Tturnaround = Tcompletion - Tarrival, Tresponse = Tfirstrun - Tarrival, the convoy effect, and 'STCF is provably optimal... SJF is optimal if all jobs arrive at the same time') match the article's formulas and claims word-for-sense. The find-the-bug exercise is a genuine, terminating bug: I traced it and P1 completes at 5, the main loop's own `while (ready.Count > 0)` condition then exits (P2 was never moved out of notArrivedYet), so the program prints 'P2 never completed' and halts — not an infinite loop — exactly as the article's solution describes, including the correct observation that a variant looping on notArrivedYet as well would spin forever. On the current-OS claims: I fetched docs.kernel.org's CFS page directly and it contains the exact quoted phrase 'CFS is making room for EEVDF'; kernelnewbies.org's 6.6 release notes independently and more bluntly state 'The previous algorithm, called CFS, was merged in Linux 2.6.23. In this release, it is replaced by code that uses a new algorithm, called EEVDF'; and kernel.org's own front page currently lists mainline at 7.3-rc4 and stable at 7.2.7 (Sept 2026), i.e. roughly three years and dozens of releases past 6.6 (Oct 2023), so this is not a claim about something bleeding-edge or reverted — it has been the shipped default for a long time. I independently fetched man7.org's sched(7) and found the exact quoted sentence 'Since Linux 2.6.23, the default scheduler is CFS, the "Completely Fair Scheduler"' still present today in the DESCRIPTION section, confirming the article's staleness callout is accurate and current, not fabricated. I fetched both Microsoft Learn pages directly: the 32-level (0-31) claim, the base-priority table entries (NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS + THREAD_PRIORITY_NORMAL = 8, HIGH_PRIORITY_CLASS + THREAD_PRIORITY_NORMAL = 13), the 0-15-only boost range, and the 'reduces that priority by one level each time the thread completes a time slice' sentence are all exact, verbatim matches to the live pages. All 9 cited sources are real and, where checked, say what the article says they say (OSTEP ch. 7 and ch. 8 PDFs, both kernel docs pages, sched(7), all three MS Learn pages, and os-book.com/OS10 which is confirmed as the real Silberschatz/Galvin/Gagne 10th-edition companion site). Differentiation is real: I pulled GeeksforGeeks's CPU-scheduling page for comparison and it is hand-worked Gantt charts with no runnable code and zero mention of what Linux or Windows currently schedule; this article's 'one simulator, one workload, five real algorithms, real measured metrics' plus a current, correctly-sourced Linux/Windows section is a genuine step up from the typical treatment (most of which, including many recently-updated pages, still say 'Linux uses CFS' unqualified).

issues.location: Round robin section, code comment above `AdmitArrivals` and the paragraph introducing it: '...or an unlucky arrival timing could let one process cut in front of another forever'
issues.problem: Overstated. Getting the admit-before-requeue order wrong changes the exact interleaving and can be locally unfair for a slice or two, but it cannot let one process 'cut in front... forever' in this non-starving, finite-workload RR — every process still gets dispatched once per pass of a bounded queue. The article's own closing exercise (find the bug) demonstrates a real, different failure mode of getting admission order wrong (permanent non-admission), which is a much better example of an actual 'forever' failure than the ordering nuance this sentence is attached to.
issues.fixLooksLike: Soften to something like 'or a process that arrived during a slice could be pushed behind an extra process it didn't need to wait behind' — accurate without implying unbounded starvation.

issues.location: Linux section, paragraph beginning 'Linux 6.6, released in 2023, replaced CFS as the default with a different algorithm, EEVDF'
issues.problem: The clean 'replaced... as the default, full stop, in 6.6' framing is well supported by kernelnewbies.org's 6.6 release notes and by docs.kernel.org's CFS page ('CFS is making room for EEVDF'), and I independently confirm the overall claim as current and accurate. But the primary source cited for this exact sentence, docs.kernel.org's own EEVDF page, is itself hedgier than the article suggests: as of today it reads 'The Linux kernel began transitioning to EEVDF in version 6.6 (as a new option in 2024)...', and LWN's April 2024 'Completing the EEVDF scheduler' piece opens with 'The EEVDF scheduler was merged as an option for the 6.6 kernel.' Neither source flatly contradicts the article, but neither is as crisp about a single-release cutover as the article implies, and the article doesn't acknowledge that the kernel's own documentation phrases it more cautiously.
issues.fixLooksLike: One clause acknowledging the transition was not instantaneous, e.g. 'Linux 6.6 (2023) began the switch from CFS to EEVDF as the default for SCHED_OTHER; by the kernels shipping today the switch is long complete' — keeps the (correct) bottom line while not overstating the precision of the kernel's own phrasing.

issues.problem: The article flags this as a paraphrase ('OSTEP states the rules this way (paraphrased...)'), which is the right move, but the wording is very close to OSTEP's own final summary of the five rules (I pulled the actual chapter-8 PDF text and the phrase-level overlap on Rules 1, 4 and 5 in particular is high — e.g. 'regardless of how many times it has given up the CPU' survives almost unchanged). Rule enumerations are hard to restate without losing precision, so this is a low-stakes case, but the closely-paraphrase rule in the editorial brief is written broadly enough that an AdSense-style critic could flag it independent of this technical review.
issues.fixLooksLike: Rephrase Rules 1, 4 and 5 in the article's own sentence structure (they already do this reasonably well for 2 and 3) so the overlap is conceptual rather than phrase-level, while keeping the attribution.
